rv.q: This household of secrets continually surprises.
Full of black comedy, this potent piece pierces the darkness.
This is a powerful piece of drama that has us leaning forward eagerly in our seats.
Bruce’s keenly observed dialogue remains vivid and raw, lifted by moments of grim humour.
‘Dixon and Daughters’ is a different kind of haunted house drama, one that builds from slow beginnings to something disturbing and memorable.
The stylistic mix feels uncomfortable in places and the play suffers from addressing a host of issues in just 90 minutes.
Still, overall, this is a well-researched and well-played piece of work, developed pre-pandemic but rendered bleakly topical by the revelations about what went on during lockdown in too many homes.
There’s lots to admire and enjoy here, but the too-neat ending, along some of the comic and dramatic flashpoints along the way, feels unearned.

It's just a pity that, in spite of a smouldering central performance by Bríd Brennan as the sour, self-pitying widow Mary, momentum is dissipated in a meandering and awkwardly staged series of confrontations.
This is an amazing feat of writing, performance and directing.
This is a dark drama sensitively interpreted.

Nevertheless, the honesty of both writing and performances shines through, making the play an involving examination of exactly why women continue to suffer in silence, in homes where they should feel safe.
Bruce's script is frank, funny, and sad, but comes to a resolution a bit too quickly.
Dixon and Daughters courses with a visceral energy that sweeps you along, even when the bald-faced emotion raises the temperature to boiling point and beyond.
Dixon and Daughters has several extremely moving moments, and both production and cast gradually create a sense of compassionate engagement with the victims of harassment and abuse.
The play is less successful at managing the overall contrasts been comedy and its darker themes.
Director Roisin McBrinn draws out the comedy to the max from the exceptional ensemble.
The fine cast negotiates the rocky path of cyclical abuse, denial and survival with speed and style under Róisin McBrinn's lively direction.
